title: 7 Best RV Generators (2026): Sized to Start Your Rooftop AC
metaDescription: The Honda EU3000iS leads 7 RV generators; plan on about 3,000 running watts to start a 13,500 BTU rooftop AC without a soft starter. Picks for 30 and 50 amp.
intro:
Seven generators for travel trailers, fifth wheels and motorhomes, chosen by the two things that actually decide the purchase: whether it starts your rooftop air conditioner, and whether it plugs into your rig without a mess of adapters.

Most RV generator advice starts with brand loyalty. It should start with one appliance. The rooftop air conditioner is the biggest, most demanding load on almost every rig, and if a generator cannot start it on a hot afternoon, nothing else on the spec sheet matters. Size for the AC first, match the plug second, and only then argue about Honda versus Champion.
quickAnswer: the Honda EU3000iS Inverter Generator is our #1 pick (best overall rv generator). The safest single-generator choice for a 30-amp trailer with one rooftop AC, if you can afford it and move it.
picksHeading: The 7 Best RV Generators in 2026, Ranked

picks.body: The EU3000iS is the generator many experienced RVers end up with after trying cheaper ones. Honda rates it at 3,000 watts maximum and 2,800 watts rated, which is enough to start and run most 13,500 BTU rooftop air conditioners along with the converter and fridge, and its TT-30R outlet means a 30-amp rig plugs in directly. Electric start makes it easy to fire up from a seat, and Honda's CO-MINDER system shuts the engine down if carbon monoxide builds up around it. The 3.4-gallon tank lets it run through a long day at moderate load, and the enclosed design keeps it quiet enough for most campgrounds. The catch is weight. At around 130 pounds, it lives on its wheels and needs a ramp or a carrier to get into a truck. If your rooftop unit is a 15,000 BTU model, add a soft starter or look one size up.
pros: Starts most 13,500 BTU rooftop units without help
Among the quietest generators in its class
Electric start and CO-MINDER automatic shutoff
TT-30R outlet, so a 30-amp rig plugs straight in
Long service life and a wide dealer network
cons: About 130 pounds; it needs wheels and a ramp
Gasoline only
Premium price compared with Champion and Westinghouse

picks.body: The iGen4500DFc takes the popular iGen4500 platform and adds dual fuel and a CO sensor, which is what the c at the end of the model name signals. Westinghouse rates it at 4,500 peak and 3,700 running watts on gasoline, comfortably above the 3,600 watts a TT-30R outlet can deliver. That surplus is the point. On a hot day or at altitude, when engine output falls, it still has enough left to start a 15,000 BTU rooftop unit and keep the converter and fridge running. Remote start lets you fire it from inside the rig, and the propane option means you can run from the tanks you already carry. Westinghouse markets it as a quiet unit at light load, and it is parallel capable if you ever outgrow it. Expect lower output on propane, and plan for its weight and size when you think about where it rides.
pros: Headroom above a TT-30R for heat and altitude
Runs on gasoline or propane
Remote start from a key fob
CO sensor with automatic shutoff
Parallel capable for larger rigs
cons: Heavy; plan on wheels and a ramp
Output drops on propane
Larger footprint than the Honda

picks.body: Champion's 4500-watt dual fuel inverter is one of the most common generators you will see parked beside travel trailers, and for good reason. Champion rates it at 4,500 starting and 3,700 running watts on gasoline, which covers a 15,000 BTU rooftop air conditioner plus everyday loads, and the dual fuel system lets you run it off a spare 20-pound cylinder instead of hauling gas cans. The TT-30R outlet plugs a 30-amp rig in directly, and electric start avoids the pull cord. It is parallel capable with compatible Champion inverters, and Champion has a broad service network and a reputation for answering the phone. The trade-offs are the usual ones for this class: it is heavy enough to need its wheels, it is a little louder than a Honda when working hard, and it makes less power on propane. For buyers who want headroom without paying Honda money, it is the default choice.

Enough output for a 15,000 BTU AC with headroom
Electric start
Parallel capable
Large U.S. service and parts network
cons: Louder than the Honda at full load
Heavy, with wheels a necessity
Propane output is lower

picks.body: The Champion 3400 is the generator that made dual fuel inverters affordable for weekend RVers. Champion rates it at 3,400 starting and 3,100 running watts on gasoline, which puts a 13,500 BTU rooftop air conditioner within reach for many rigs, especially with a soft starter fitted. It has a TT-30R outlet, electric start on most versions, and the ability to run on propane from your RV tanks, so you can leave the gas can at home. Champion builds parallel capability in, so a second inverter can be added later. Where it falls short is headroom. A 15,000 BTU unit, a hot afternoon or a campground at elevation can push it to its limit, and when it works hard, it gets louder. It is also heavy for its output. Buy it for a mid-size trailer with one 13,500 BTU AC, not for a big rig with every appliance running.

Lower price than any single-unit pick here
cons: Little headroom for a 15,000 BTU unit

Propane output is noticeably lower

picks.body: The EU2200i is the best-known small inverter generator in the country, and for RV owners it works as half of a system. Honda rates one unit at 2,200 watts maximum and 1,800 rated, enough to charge batteries, run the fridge on electric, a microwave and lights. With a soft starter on the AC, many owners report it starting a 13,500 BTU unit, though that is at the edge. Paralleled with a second EU2200i, the pair delivers about 4,400 starting and 3,600 running watts, which matches a 30-amp rig, and Honda's parallel hardware or the EU2200i Companion model provides the TT-30R outlet. At about 47 pounds each, the halves are easy to load, and CO-MINDER shuts each engine down if CO builds up. The pair costs more than one big inverter, but no other path gives you this much flexibility from mild weekends to hot summers.

Two in parallel give 3,600 running watts for a 30-amp rig
Very quiet at light load
CO-MINDER automatic shutoff
Doubles as a camping and tailgating generator
cons: One alone will not reliably start a rooftop AC without a soft starter
A pair plus kit costs more than a single 4,500W inverter
Gasoline only

picks.body: If your fifth wheel or motorhome has a 50-amp plug and you want every appliance running at once, you need a generator with a 14-50R outlet, and that means a big open-frame machine like the WGen9500DF. Westinghouse rates it at 12,500 peak and 9,500 running watts on gasoline, enough for two rooftop air conditioners, the residential fridge and the microwave together. It runs on gasoline or propane and has remote electric start. The downsides are serious for camping. It is an open-frame conventional generator, so it is far louder than any inverter on this list, and many campgrounds and parks will not allow it. It weighs far more than one person can lift and needs a trailer or a cargo carrier. Buy it for remote boondocking or because you also want serious home backup. For park camping, a 30-amp dogbone and a quiet 4,500-watt inverter make a better pairing.

Enough output to run two rooftop air conditioners

picks.body: The SOLIX F3800 is the way to camp with power during quiet hours and in generator-free loops. Anker rates its LFP battery at 3,840Wh and its inverter at 6,000 watts, and it carries a TT-30R outlet, so a 30-amp rig plugs straight in and runs everything, including a rooftop air conditioner, without a sound. The limit is capacity. An AC drawing around 1,400 watts drains it in a few hours, so on its own it is an overnight and quiet-hours solution, not an all-day one. It shines as half of a hybrid: run the battery through the night, then recharge it from solar panels or a small inverter generator during allowed hours. It also expands with add-on batteries for longer runs. At around 132 pounds it rides on its wheels and stays in the rig or truck. Because it makes no exhaust, it can sit beside the trailer rather than 20 feet away.

sections.heading: Sizing for the Rooftop Air Conditioner
sections.body:
A typical 13,500 BTU rooftop unit draws somewhere around 1,200 to 1,600 watts once the compressor is running, depending on the brand, the outside temperature and how hard it is working. A 15,000 BTU unit runs higher, commonly 1,500 to 1,900 watts. Those running numbers look easy for a 2,200-watt generator. The problem is the first second, when the compressor motor starts against pressure and briefly pulls several times its running current.

That start surge is what kills small-generator plans. Depending on the unit, a 13,500 BTU compressor can momentarily demand 2,500 to 3,500 watts or more, and an older or tired compressor can be worse. An inverter generator responds by sagging, stalling or tripping its overload. This is why a single 2,200-watt inverter starting a rooftop AC without help is a coin toss, and why owners who say it works are often camping at sea level on a mild day.

A soft starter changes the math. Devices such as the Micro-Air EasyStart and SoftStartRV are wired into the air conditioner and ramp the compressor up instead of slamming it on, which makers say cuts the start surge by more than half. With one installed, many owners report a 13,500 BTU unit starting reliably on a 2,200-watt inverter, and a 15,000 BTU unit starting comfortably on a 3,000-watt-class generator. Installation takes an hour or two for a handy owner, or a short shop visit.

Without a soft starter, a sensible floor is about 3,000 running watts for a 13,500 BTU unit and 3,500 or more for a 15,000 BTU unit, which is why the 3,000 to 4,500-watt class dominates this list. Remember the AC never runs alone. The converter charging your house batteries, the fridge on electric mode, a coffee maker or a microwave all stack on top. A 30-amp rig tops out around 3,600 watts anyway, so that is the target most travel trailer owners are actually shopping for.

Altitude and heat both cut generator output. Engines lose roughly 3 to 4 percent of their power per 1,000 feet of elevation, so a generator that just barely starts your AC in Florida may refuse in Colorado. If you camp high or in the desert in July, buy a size up or install the soft starter regardless of which generator you choose. It is the cheapest insurance in RV power.

sections.heading: 30-Amp, 50-Amp and the Adapters Between
sections.body:
Look at the end of your RV's shore power cord before you look at generators. A 30-amp rig has a three-prong plug that fits a NEMA TT-30R outlet: 120 volts, 30 amps, about 3,600 watts maximum. A 50-amp rig has a four-prong plug that fits a NEMA 14-50R: two 120-volt legs at 50 amps each, about 12,000 watts in total. Nearly every RV-ready inverter generator has a TT-30R on the panel. Very few portables have a 14-50R, and those that do are big, loud, open-frame machines.

The good news for 50-amp owners is that you do not need 12,000 watts to camp. A 50-amp-to-30-amp adapter, often called a dogbone, lets a 50-amp rig plug into a TT-30R generator. You then live within 3,600 watts: one air conditioner, not two, and no microwave while the AC is cycling. Many 50-amp fifth wheels have an energy management system that sheds loads automatically when it detects a 30-amp supply, which makes this arrangement easy to live with.

The adapter question gets dangerous with 240-volt outlets. A generator's L14-30R twist-lock is a 120/240-volt outlet, and an adapter from it to a TT-30 plug must take only one 120-volt leg, which means your RV sees only half of the generator's output. Mis-wired or improvised adapters that send 240 volts into a TT-30 rig can destroy the converter, the fridge board and anything else plugged in. Buy a molded, labeled adapter, never a homemade one, and never confuse a TT-30R with a 240-volt NEMA 10-30 dryer outlet.

Searches for a 30 amp RV plug adapter usually come from the opposite problem: plugging the rig into a household 15 or 20-amp outlet or a small generator with only standard receptacles. Those puck-style adapters work, but they limit you to roughly 1,800 to 2,400 watts, which will run lights, the converter and a fridge on electric, not the air conditioner. One more detail: many inverter generators have a floating neutral, and some RV surge protectors read that as an open ground and refuse to pass power. A neutral-ground bonding plug in a spare outlet solves it.

| Plug | Outlet | Voltage | Usable watts |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| 30-amp RV | NEMA TT-30R | 120V | About 3,600W |
| 50-amp RV | NEMA 14-50R | 120/240V | About 12,000W |
| 50A rig on 30A dogbone | NEMA TT-30R | 120V | About 3,600W |
| 30A rig on household puck | 5-15R / 5-20R | 120V | About 1,800-2,400W |

sections.heading: Side-by-Side Comparison
sections.body:
The table below lines up the seven picks on the specs that matter for RV use. Watts are the manufacturer's gasoline ratings where we are confident of them. Rather than reprint a decibel figure for every machine, we have grouped them by noise class, because makers measure at different loads and the differences between neighboring numbers are small next to the difference between an inverter and an open-frame generator.

| Model | Gas watts (start / run) | RV outlet | Fuel | Noise class |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Honda EU3000iS | 3,000 / 2,800 | TT-30R | Gas | Very quiet inverter |
| Westinghouse iGen4500DFc | 4,500 / 3,700 | TT-30R | Gas or propane | Quiet inverter |
| Champion 4500W Dual Fuel | 4,500 / 3,700 | TT-30R | Gas or propane | Quiet inverter |
| Champion 3400W Dual Fuel | 3,400 / 3,100 | TT-30R | Gas or propane | Quiet inverter |
| Honda EU2200i (pair) | 4,400 / 3,600 paralleled | TT-30R via kit | Gas | Very quiet inverter |
| Westinghouse WGen9500DF | 12,500 / 9,500 | 14-50R | Gas or propane | Loud open frame |
| Anker SOLIX F3800 | 6,000W continuous | TT-30R | Battery | Silent |

Two patterns jump out. First, the 3,000 to 4,500-watt inverters all land at or just above the 3,600 watts a TT-30R can deliver, which is why they are the default choice for 30-amp trailers. Buying more generator than your plug can carry only buys you headroom for altitude and heat, which is useful, but beyond that it is weight and fuel you are hauling for nothing.

Second, the only way to feed a 50-amp rig at full capacity from a portable is an open-frame generator like the WGen9500DF, and that comes with noise most campgrounds will not tolerate. If you camp in parks with neighbors, a 50-amp rig on a dogbone and a quiet 4,500-watt inverter is the better combination. Save the big open-frame unit for boondocking far from anyone else, or for home backup.

Weight is the hidden spec. The single-unit 3,000 to 4,500-watt inverters all sit around 100 to 130 pounds, which means wheels, a ramp or a hitch-mounted carrier. If you cannot lift one into a truck bed, the parallel pair of EU2200i units, at about 47 pounds each, is the practical answer, even though it costs more for the same output.

sections.heading: Parallel Kits: Two Small Generators vs One Big One
sections.body:
Parallel capability lets you link two compatible inverter generators with a short cable kit so they combine their output into one outlet. Two Honda EU2200i units paralleled deliver 4,400 starting and 3,600 running watts, which lines up exactly with a 30-amp RV. The parallel kit usually includes or sits beside a TT-30R outlet, so the rig plugs straight in. Honda also sells an EU2200i Companion model that carries the TT-30R on its own panel.

The case for a pair is flexibility. On a cool weekend, you bring one generator, charge the batteries and run the microwave. When the forecast says 95 degrees, you bring both and run the air conditioner. Each half weighs about 47 pounds, so one person can load them. And if one generator develops a problem far from a shop, you still have half your power instead of none.

The case against is cost and complexity. Two premium 2,200-watt generators plus a parallel kit cost meaningfully more than a single 3,000 to 4,500-watt dual fuel inverter, you maintain two engines, and you carry two sets of fuel. Most parallel kits require two of the same model or the same brand family; you generally cannot mix a Honda with a Champion. Check the manufacturer's compatibility list before buying a second unit to match one you already own.

Our rule of thumb: if you can handle a 100-plus pound generator with wheels and you always need air conditioning, buy one bigger inverter. If you cannot lift that much, camp in mixed weather, or also want a small generator for tailgating and tent trips, buy one 2,200-watt unit now and add its twin later. That second path also overlaps neatly with our [camping generator picks](/best-generator-for-camping/), which cover the small end of the market in more depth.

sections.heading: Dual Fuel and Running Off the RV's Propane
sections.body:
Most RVs already carry propane, either in two 20 or 30-pound cylinders on a travel trailer tongue or in a permanently mounted ASME tank on a motorhome. A dual fuel generator can draw from that supply, which means no separate gas cans in the truck bed, no stale gasoline gumming the carburetor over the winter, and one fuel to refill at the campground store. For a lot of owners, that alone justifies choosing dual fuel.

The trade-off is output. Propane carries less energy per unit than gasoline, so every dual fuel generator is rated lower on propane, commonly by around 10 percent. That matters when your sizing is already tight. A dual fuel unit that starts your 15,000 BTU air conditioner on gasoline may struggle on propane on a hot day. Check the propane running watts on the spec sheet, not the headline gasoline number, if you plan to run on LP most of the time.

Running from RV tanks takes the right hardware. On a travel trailer, the simplest method is a propane hose from the generator to a spare 20-pound cylinder, or an extended-stay tee at the tank valve. On a motorhome with an ASME tank, a quick-connect port installed by an RV technician is the clean solution. Use hose rated for the purpose, check connections with soapy water, and keep the line short and out of foot traffic.

Propane also burns through tanks faster than people expect. A generator working hard to run an air conditioner can empty a 20-pound cylinder in well under a day of continuous use, so budget for it, and remember that same tank feeds your furnace and fridge. In cold weather, propane vapor pressure drops and small cylinders can struggle to keep up with demand. For winter camping, gasoline or a larger tank is the more reliable fuel.

sections.heading: Quiet Hours, Campground Rules and Decibels
sections.body:
Generator noise is quoted in dB(A), usually measured at 7 meters, about 23 feet. The scale is logarithmic: every 10 dB step sounds roughly twice as loud to the human ear. A quality inverter at light load in the high 40s to low 50s is closer to conversation than to a lawn mower. An open-frame generator in the 70s is a different experience entirely, and your neighbors will hear the difference before you do.

Campgrounds regulate generators more than most first-time owners expect. Quiet hours commonly run from 10 p.m. to 6 or 8 a.m., and many state and national park campgrounds go further, allowing generators only in set windows and banning them in tent or walk-in loops. National Park Service rules cap generator noise at 60 dB(A) measured at 50 feet, and individual parks set their own hours. Check the campground page or call ahead, because rules vary loop by loop.

Load changes noise more than brand does. Every inverter on this list is rated quietest at a quarter load, and gets louder as the air conditioner cycles on and the engine ramps up. A generator running near its limit to hold a 15,000 BTU AC will be several decibels louder than its brochure figure. Buying a size up, or adding a soft starter so the generator idles more of the time, is the practical route to a quieter site.

Placement helps too. Point the exhaust away from your rig and your neighbors, keep the generator on gravel or a mat rather than a hollow truck bed that acts like a drum, and use a longer heavy-gauge cord to put distance between the generator and where people sit. Never build an enclosure that traps exhaust; the heat and carbon monoxide hazards outweigh any noise benefit.

sections.heading: Power Station Hybrids and Solar
sections.body:
Large battery power stations have changed RV power more than any generator in the last few years. A unit like the Anker SOLIX F3800 plugs into a 30-amp rig through its own TT-30R outlet and runs the rig silently, through quiet hours and in generator-free loops. Our guide to the [best portable power stations](/best-portable-power-station/) covers the wider field, and it is worth reading before you assume a generator is the only answer.

The limit is energy, not power. A rooftop air conditioner drawing 1,400 watts empties a 3,840Wh battery in well under three hours. Batteries excel at everything else: overnight fans, the furnace blower, the water pump, lights, a CPAP and the fridge on 12-volt or electric. The smartest RV systems run the battery through the night and quiet hours, then run a generator for an hour or two during the day to refill it and cool the rig.

Solar closes the gap further for boondockers. Several hundred watts of folding panels can put back a meaningful share of a day's battery use in good sun, and our picks for the [best portable solar panels](/best-portable-solar-panel/) and the [best solar generators](/best-solar-generator/) show how to size the array to the battery. Solar will not run a rooftop AC in practice, but it can cut generator hours sharply.

If your rig already has a lithium house battery bank, a separate power station may be redundant. In that case the upgrade is a larger inverter and more lithium capacity built into the RV itself; our guide to the [best power inverters](/best-power-inverter/) covers that route. Either way, pairing batteries with a smaller quiet generator is now usually a better plan than buying the biggest generator you can lift.

sections.heading: Carbon Monoxide and Setup at the Campsite
sections.body:
A portable generator produces carbon monoxide, an odorless gas that kills campers every year. Run it outdoors only: never inside the RV, a basement storage bay, an enclosed truck bed with a cap, a tent or under a closed awning. Keep it as far from the rig as your cord allows, the U.S. Consumer Product Safety Commission recommends at least 20 feet from occupied spaces, with the exhaust pointed away from doors, windows, roof vents and your neighbor's site.

Buy a generator with automatic CO shutoff. Honda calls it CO-MINDER, Champion calls it CO Shield and Westinghouse uses a CO sensor on models with a trailing c, such as the iGen4500DFc. These systems shut the engine down when CO builds up around the generator. They are a backstop for bad placement and changing wind, not a substitute for distance, and they do nothing about exhaust drifting into a parked rig through an open window.

Inside the RV, a working CO alarm is non-negotiable. Most RVs come with one, but alarms have a service life, commonly in the five to ten-year range, and many owners never check the date. Test it before every trip and replace it at end of life. Pay particular attention when the rig is parked downwind or close to another camper's generator, because their exhaust is your problem too.

Two more setup habits matter. Let the generator cool before refueling, since spilled gasoline on a hot muffler is a fire risk. And run your shore cord through a surge protector or energy management system, which protects the rig from voltage swings and, on 50-amp rigs, from a mis-wired adapter. A good EMS is cheap compared with replacing a converter or a fridge control board.

sections.heading: Which One to Buy
sections.body:
For a 30-amp travel trailer with one 13,500 BTU air conditioner and a buyer who wants the least drama, buy the **Honda EU3000iS**. It starts most 13,500 BTU units on its own, runs quietly through long afternoons and has the strongest reputation for longevity on this list. If budget matters more than the Honda badge, the **Champion 3400W Dual Fuel** gets you a similar result on gasoline and lets you burn the propane already on your tongue.

For a 15,000 BTU unit, a hot climate or high elevation, step up to the **Westinghouse iGen4500DFc** or the **Champion 4500W Dual Fuel**. Both give you headroom above the 3,600 watts a TT-30R can carry, which is what you want when heat and altitude eat into output. Choose the Westinghouse for its remote start and generally quieter reputation, the Champion for its wide service network.

If you cannot lift 100 pounds, buy one **Honda EU2200i** now, add a soft starter to the air conditioner, and buy a second unit with a parallel kit when you need more. If you own a 50-amp fifth wheel and boondock far from anyone, the **Westinghouse WGen9500DF** runs both air conditioners at once. If you mostly stay in parks with strict generator rules, the **Anker SOLIX F3800** may serve you better than any engine.

The generator we would skip for RV use is any cheap open-frame unit in the 3,000 to 4,000-watt range. They are loud enough to get you complaints, they often lack a TT-30R, and the raw power is less clean for the rig's electronics. If you also want the same machine to back up the house, read our [home generators for power outages](/best-home-generator-for-power-outages/) guide before you decide; the right answer for a driveway is often wrong for a campground.

mistakes.title: Sizing to the running watts alone
mistakes.body: A 13,500 BTU rooftop unit may run on 1,400 watts but demand twice that or more for the first second of a compressor start. Sizing to the running number is why so many 2,200-watt generators stall on hot afternoons. Size to the start surge, or fit a soft starter and size to the running load.

mistakes.title: Using a homemade 240-volt adapter
mistakes.body: Adapters from an L14-30R or a dryer outlet to a TT-30 plug must deliver one 120-volt leg only. Improvised or mis-wired ones can send 240 volts into a 30-amp rig and destroy the converter and fridge board in an instant. Buy a molded, labeled adapter and run the rig through a surge protector.

mistakes.title: Ignoring the propane derating
mistakes.body: Every dual fuel generator makes less power on propane. If your sizing only just works on gasoline, it may fail on propane, especially in heat or at altitude. Read the propane running watts on the spec sheet before relying on your RV tanks as the main fuel for air conditioning.

mistakes.title: Running the generator too close to the rig
mistakes.body: Parking the generator under the awning or beside an open window lets carbon monoxide drift inside. Keep it outdoors, as far away as your cord allows, at least 20 feet from occupied spaces where possible, exhaust pointed away, and test the RV's CO alarm before every trip. Watch neighbors' exhaust too.

mistakes.title: Skipping the campground rules
mistakes.body: Many parks restrict generator hours, ban them in some loops, or cap noise at 60 dB(A) at 50 feet. Showing up with a loud open-frame generator can mean a long, hot weekend. Read the campground page before you book, and choose an inverter quiet enough for the places you actually camp.

faqs.q: What size generator do I need to run a 13,500 BTU RV air conditioner?
faqs.a: Without a soft starter, plan on about 3,000 running watts so the compressor can start reliably along with the converter and fridge. With a soft starter installed, many owners report a single 2,200-watt inverter starting a 13,500 BTU unit, though that leaves little margin. Heat and altitude both reduce generator output, so buy a size up if you camp in the desert or the mountains.

faqs.q: Can a 50-amp RV run on a 30-amp generator?
faqs.a: Yes. A 50-to-30-amp dogbone adapter lets a 50-amp rig plug into a TT-30R generator outlet. You are then limited to about 3,600 watts, which typically means one air conditioner and careful use of the microwave and water heater on electric. Many 50-amp rigs have an energy management system that automatically sheds loads on a 30-amp supply, which makes the arrangement easy to live with.

faqs.q: What is a 30 amp RV plug adapter used for?
faqs.a: It usually adapts the rig's TT-30 plug to a standard 15 or 20-amp household outlet, or to a generator without a TT-30R. That works for lights, the converter and a fridge on electric, but limits you to roughly 1,800 to 2,400 watts, so the air conditioner is off the table. Adapters from 240-volt outlets need care; buy molded, labeled ones only.

faqs.q: Is dual fuel worth it for an RV generator?
faqs.a: For most RVers, yes. Running from the propane already on board eliminates gas cans, avoids stale fuel over the winter and simplifies refueling. The cost is lower output on propane, commonly around 10 percent, and faster tank use than many people expect. If your sizing is tight, check the propane running watts before relying on LP for air conditioning on hot days.

faqs.q: Can I run my RV generator overnight at a campground?
faqs.a: Usually not. Most campgrounds enforce quiet hours, commonly from around 10 p.m. to the morning, and many state and national parks restrict generators to set daytime windows. A battery power station or the rig's own lithium bank is the way to keep fans, the furnace blower and a CPAP running overnight, recharged by the generator during allowed hours.

faqs.q: Are portable power stations for RVs good enough to replace a generator?
faqs.a: For quiet hours, light loads and short trips with hookups between, they can be. A large unit with a TT-30R outlet runs the whole rig silently, but a rooftop AC drains even a 3,840Wh battery in a few hours. For multi-day boondocking with air conditioning, most owners still need a generator, ideally a small quiet one paired with the battery and solar.

faqs.q: How far should an RV generator be from the camper?
faqs.a: As far as practical. The CPSC recommends at least 20 feet from occupied spaces for portable generators, with the exhaust pointed away from doors, windows and roof vents. At a tight campsite that can be hard, so use a longer heavy-gauge cord, buy a generator with automatic CO shutoff, and keep a working CO alarm inside the rig.

bottomLine:
Buy an RV generator by working backward from the rooftop air conditioner and the plug on your shore cord. For most 30-amp trailers, that leads to a 3,000 to 4,500-watt inverter with a TT-30R outlet, ideally dual fuel, and a soft starter on the AC for margin.

Then think about the hours you cannot run it. A battery power station or a lithium house bank covers quiet hours and nights, and a quiet generator refills it during the day. That combination keeps you cool, keeps the neighbors friendly and keeps carbon monoxide well away from where you sleep.
